items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Connie was a reasonable fellow but did not stand for his show people to be abused.

ctx.x: But Connie's was beginning to lose the white clients from downtown because Harlem was turning bad and so many white people were getting robbed when they came uptown. And negros, the few that ever went to the place, were treated so bad they got the tables where it was almost impossible to see the floor show, so they did not come there when the place started losing the white customers. This happened in 1933. I had rejoined Russell in 1932.

We doubled in some theaters including the Lafayette and that was hard work because we would be in the theaters all day from 11 a.m. until 11 at night and then have to come to the Inn and do two shows. We were paid on time for doing the shows but not at the Inn and each week Connie was getting deeper in debt to the band and the other folks in the show.
